theme: 宠物-工作犬野外走失事件

content.text: Shi Yan, look, these are the photos of the emergency recall training I've been doing with Lightning these past few days. After the last incident, I've reflected deeply and realized I can't let him run around freely anymore.

Hmm, in the photo, Lightning is sitting very attentively, and the direction you're pointing with your finger is also very clear. There's progress in training, but relying solely on commands isn't enough.
Yes, I was just about to ask you. Watching the stone video you shared earlier, it’s almost as obedient as your shadow. How did you train it to be so well-behaved?

This is not just about command training; it's about building a collaborative team relationship. It's about helping the dog understand the goals and rules of our joint actions, much like the teamwork we emphasized during our previous hiking trips.
Team collaboration? That sounds profound. How exactly do you do it? When I take Lightning out, I usually let him explore freely while I take my photos.

Yes, just like when we discussed gear in Session 2, I suggested sharing the load. You have to make Lightning understand that outdoor activities are a team effort. I use consistent signals, like specific whistles and gestures, to let him know when to come close and when he can explore.
The whistle and hand signals... this reminds me of Session 3 when we established communication protocols, also using consistent signals to avoid confusion. So, should we do the same for dogs?

Absolutely. The core value of safety first applies not only to people but also to pets. I suggest you conduct progressive training in high-distraction environments, such as when other animals are present, starting from low-risk situations.

High-interference environment... Lightning got distracted by small animals in the meadow last time and ran off. I need to strengthen training in this area. Also, technical backups are important, right?

Yes, just as we discussed in Session 3 about satellite phones as a last resort. This is a screenshot of the GPS tracker product I mentioned earlier, which allows real-time location tracking to avoid the frantic search like last time.
This looks quite practical! I've decided to adopt it as a technical backup. However, relying solely on equipment isn't enough; we also need to focus on prevention at the root.

Yes, practicality comes first. But when taking pets outdoors, there are also ethical and responsibility issues. We must satisfy their natural instincts, just as you value the beauty of nature, while also ensuring their safety and not disturbing wildlife.

I completely agree. The principle of leaving no trace applies not only to the environment but also to pet behavior. Lightning's disappearance might have also disturbed the local wildlife. I need to be more responsible.

Look at this photo, when Stone interacts with me, it always stays within controllable limits. This requires long-term training and building trust, just like our relationship from Session 1 to now, evolving from strangers to caring for each other.

Yes, from route consultation to knee injury recovery, and now this pet incident, you've always provided me with professional guidance. I now better understand the importance of safety redundancy, just like what you emphasized in Session 4: 'Stability is more important than speed.'

Team collaboration is a two-way street. From sharing your recovery experience in Session 5 to actively training this time, I’ve also seen your adaptability and progress. As for the lightning incident, let’s learn from it together.

Thank you! I will develop a systematic training plan and incorporate GPS trackers to enhance the safety of future outdoor activities with Lightning. How has your knee injury been lately? Have you continued managing it after Session 7?
Much better, the daily aches have lessened a lot, thanks to the swimming you recommended. Now I’m also applying this preventive mindset to handling stones to reduce the risk of accidents.
Great! Then it's settled: I'll intensify the training for Lightning, and you'll continue with the rehabilitation management. Next time outdoors, I hope it will be safer and more harmonious.
Well, learning from incidents, formulating and implementing preventive measures—that's the true embodiment of respecting nature and teamwork. Stay in touch and share updates anytime.
